newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba starts meeting, revaluation tops agenda.
newsitem.headline: Buba starts meeting, revaluation tops agenda.

text.p: The Bundesbank's central policymaking council started its regular fortnightly meeting on Thursday with its agenda topped by a controversial revaluation of its currency reserves.

Bundesbank officials have said the meeting will discuss the revaluation of certain central bank assets after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer and Finance Minister Theo Waigel said they were close to resolving their dispute over the matter.
Financial markets are expecting the Bundesbank to make some kind of statement but it is unclear whether the bank will actually do so.
Six out of 10 analysts polled by Reuters on Tuesday said they expected the Bundesbank to approve a compromise solution.
Waigel last week backed down from a plan to seek a special payout in 1997 from a revaluation of reserves held at the Bundesbank.
The plan was widely seen as an attempt to fudge the Maastricht Treaty's convergence criteria to enable Germany to qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
The Bundesbank condemned it in a sharply-worded statement as risking the credibility of the planned single currency.

Under a compromise plan, the Bundesbank will revalue part of its currency reserves in 1997 and make a special payout in 1998 to the Inherited Debt Redemption Fund, thereby helping to reduce Germany's public debt.
Such a payout would come too late to help Germany reduce its debt in 1997 -- the key year for deciding which nations can join EMU, scheduled to start in January 1999.
The revaluation is not expected to affect the Bundesbank's gold reserves.
Economists said they do not expect the Bundesbank to change interest rates at Thursday's meeting.
